name: HOMS Assessment Design Law
principles: Assessment format follows the canonical CAPS ontology, not a generic exam template.
Every generated visual must serve an assessment purpose: stimulus, learner workspace, teacher scoring aid, or moderation evidence.
Foundation phase prioritises concrete, observable, low-reading-load visuals.
Intermediate phase prioritises labelled diagrams, process charts, tables, and visible reasoning scaffolds.
Senior and FET phases may use richer diagrams, tables, grids, source panels, and rubric matrices when the ontology allows it.
Long essays, source packs, business case studies, and formal exam layouts are default-off unless the subject profile allows them.
A human educator must approve the final visual and marking interpretation before classroom use.

document_style.page_note: Educator approval required before classroom use.

rules: Use large labels and simple shapes.
Keep learner reading load minimal.
Prefer manipulatives, cards, number lines, matching grids, and picture prompts.
Show workspace and method marks.
Use grids, axes, diagrams, or tables when the question requires visible reasoning.
Do not turn calculations into essay prompts.
Use readable data tables and labelled diagrams.
Separate observation, interpretation, and conclusion.
Flag safety or method controls where practical work appears.
Keep the case scenario compact.
Use tables for facts, stakeholders, numbers, and recommendations.
Memo must accept justified alternatives where appropriate.
Show design, build, test, improve as a visible workflow.
Use labelled diagrams and test log tables.
State safety, materials, constraints, and deliverables.
Use observable criteria.
Make performance space, process, and reflection visible.
Rubric levels must be readable and teacher-facing.
Separate reading/viewing, writing/presenting, language structures, and oral/listening.
Scale text length to grade.
Do not import subject-case-study structure unless the language task needs it.
Sources must be visibly separated from questions.
Use claim/evidence/reasoning tables.
Keep extended responses scaffolded for younger phases.
